people.name: Fredrick L. McGhee
body: In 1889 a young lawyer who had been born into slavery near Aberdeen, Mississippi, was admitted to the bar in Minnesota. With that, Fredrick McGhee became the first African American lawyer in Minnesota. He had come north to St. Paul, part of a small but growing Black community that would later center on the Rondo neighborhood.

To understand McGhee, it helps to know the era. The promises of Reconstruction had collapsed in the South, and Jim Crow laws were spreading. Black Americans who moved north were looking for work, safety, and a fair hearing. Even in Minnesota, they met discrimination in housing, hotels, and jobs. Leaders such as McGhee built the institutions that helped the community push back.

McGhee became known as a skilled criminal defense lawyer whose courtroom wins made headlines. Outside the courtroom, he turned to building community. Within a few years of arriving he had become Catholic, and he co-founded St. Peter Claver, St. Paul's Black Catholic parish, with Archbishop John Ireland.

His influence also reached far beyond Minnesota. In 1905 he was one of the men who joined W. E. B. Du Bois in founding the Niagara Movement. The group demanded full civil and political rights for Black Americans at a time when many national voices urged patience. The Niagara Movement became the forerunner of the National Association for the Advancement of Colored People (NAACP), founded in 1909, and McGhee led the effort to establish an NAACP chapter in Minnesota. In March 1912 he and others formed the Twin City Protective League, which voted to affiliate with the NAACP. Colleagues carried the work forward after his death, and the St. Paul branch received its charter in 1913. He died in 1912, a few weeks before his 51st birthday, after an accident at his cabin on the Apple River in Wisconsin.

McGhee's legacy lives in the institutions he helped build: a church, a civil rights chapter, and a national movement. His life shows that Minnesota's Black community was an active part of the national struggle for civil rights from its earliest days.
keyFacts: 1861: Born enslaved near Aberdeen, Mississippi.
1889: Moved to St. Paul and became Minnesota's first African American lawyer.
Co-founded St. Peter Claver Catholic Church in St. Paul.
1905: Among the founders of the Niagara Movement with W. E. B. Du Bois.
Led the effort to establish Minnesota's first NAACP chapter.
1912: Died after an accident at his Wisconsin cabin.

people.name: Lena Olive Smith
body: In 1931 a Black family, Arthur and Edith Lee, bought a house in a mostly white neighborhood in South Minneapolis. Crowds gathered outside the home to pressure them to leave. When a white attorney dropped out, the family's lawyer became Lena Olive Smith. She was the first African American woman licensed to practice law in Minnesota, and she defended their right to live where they chose.

Smith had moved to Minneapolis from Kansas in 1907. She graduated from Northwestern College of Law and became a lawyer in 1921. According to MNopedia, she remained the only Black woman practicing law in the state until 1945. Housing discrimination would become one of the defining issues of her career.

Housing discrimination in Minneapolis was organized and widespread. Racial covenants written into property deeds barred Black families from buying homes in many neighborhoods. The pattern shaped where Black Minneapolitans could live, attend school, and build wealth, and its effects are still visible in the city today. Smith was among those who fought it at the time, in court and in the community.

She also helped build the organizations that served the community. In 1925 she helped found the Minneapolis chapter of the Urban League, which focused on jobs and housing. In 1930 she became the first woman president of the Minneapolis NAACP, serving nine years. In that role she challenged police brutality, winning a 1937 case for a man beaten by two off-duty detectives. She also led the NAACP protest against a 1940 University of Minnesota showing of the racist film The Birth of a Nation.
Smith was still practicing law when she died in 1966 at age 81. Her work is part of a long tradition of Black Minnesotans using the law to claim rights the state's own laws promised.
keyFacts: 1885: Born.
1907: Moved to Minneapolis from Kansas.
1921: Graduated from Northwestern College of Law and became Minnesota's first African American woman lawyer.
1925: Helped found the Minneapolis Urban League.
1930: Became first woman president of the Minneapolis NAACP; served nine years.
1931: Defended the Lee family against mob pressure in South Minneapolis.
1966: Died, still practicing law.

people.name: Nellie Stone Johnson
body: In 1935, Nellie Stone Johnson, an elevator operator at the Minneapolis Athletic Club, began signing up her coworkers. A new federal law had protected workers' right to organize, and the club had cut food workers' pay from $15.00 to $12.50 a week. Nellie Stone Johnson and her fellow organizers helped unionize downtown hotel workers, and the club's integrated Local 665 of the Hotel and Restaurant Employees union was soon chartered. In 1936 she was elected its vice president. It was the start of a lifetime of organizing.

Johnson was born to farmers in Dakota County and grew up on a dairy farm in Pine County, where she helped her father organize for the Nonpartisan League. She moved to Minneapolis around 1922 to finish high school. She saw a direct connection between fair pay and civil rights: Black workers were often shut out of good jobs, and unions could be a path to economic security if they were open to everyone. She worked to make sure they were.

She was also involved in politics at a key moment. In 1944 Minnesota's Democratic Party and Farmer-Labor Party merged to form the Democratic-Farmer-Labor Party (DFL). Johnson helped bring the merger about. She became an ally of Hubert Humphrey, who sought her support in his mayoral campaigns, and she helped create Minneapolis's first Fair Employment Commission and pass Minnesota's fair employment and fair housing laws.

In 1945 Johnson was elected to the Minneapolis Library Board, becoming the first Black person elected to citywide office in Minneapolis. After retiring from the hotel industry in 1963, she ran her own alterations shop in downtown Minneapolis for decades while continuing her activism. In 1987 she was appointed to the State University Board.
Her legacy is visible today. A Minneapolis public school carries her name, and the History Theatre in St. Paul has staged a play about her life.
keyFacts: 1905: Born in Dakota County; grew up on a Pine County dairy farm.
1935: Helped organize hotel workers; Local 665 chartered soon after.
1936: Elected vice president of Local 665.
1944: Helped bring about the merger that created the Minnesota DFL Party.
1945: Elected to the Minneapolis Library Board, the first Black person elected to citywide office in Minneapolis.
1963: Opened her own alterations shop in downtown Minneapolis.
1987: Appointed to the State University Board.
2002: Died at age 96.
A Minneapolis public school is named in her honor.

people.name: Roy Wilkins
body: In 1920, three Black circus workers were lynched by a mob in Duluth, Minnesota. Roy Wilkins was a University of Minnesota student at the time, and he later wrote that the killings ended his innocence about race. They showed him that racial violence was not limited to the South. He went on to become one of the most important civil rights leaders in American history.

Wilkins was born in St. Louis. After his mother died, he was raised by relatives in St. Paul, where he attended an integrated school. He studied at the University of Minnesota and wrote for the student newspaper, the Minnesota Daily. In 1921 he joined the St. Paul branch of the NAACP. He graduated in 1923.

After college, Wilkins edited the Kansas City Call, an important Black weekly newspaper. In 1931 he joined the national staff of the NAACP in New York as assistant secretary. In 1934 he succeeded W. E. B. Du Bois as editor of its magazine, The Crisis. He became acting head in 1949 and executive secretary in 1955. He led the NAACP until 1977, a period that included the Montgomery Bus Boycott, the 1963 March on Washington, and the passage of the Civil Rights Act of 1964 and the Voting Rights Act of 1965.

Wilkins believed in changing the country through courts, laws, and the ballot. He worked with presidents and members of Congress to pass civil rights legislation. Younger activists sometimes criticized his cautious style, but his patient work helped secure some of the most important legal protections in American history.
He died in 1981. In 1984 the St. Paul Civic Center Auditorium was renamed the Roy Wilkins Auditorium.
keyFacts: 1901: Born in St. Louis; raised by relatives in St. Paul.
1921: Joined the St. Paul NAACP branch.
1923: Graduated from the University of Minnesota, where he wrote for the Minnesota Daily.
1931: Joined the national NAACP staff as assistant secretary.
1934: Became editor of The Crisis.
1949–1977: Led the NAACP (acting executive secretary from 1949; executive secretary 1955; title became executive director in 1964).
1981: Died.
1984: St. Paul auditorium renamed in his honor.

people.name: Gordon Parks
body: In 1942, in Washington, D.C., Gordon Parks photographed Ella Watson, a Black government charwoman. She stood in front of an American flag holding a broom and mop. The picture, known as American Gothic after Grant Wood's painting, became one of the most famous images of segregation-era America. The quiet portrait asked viewers to see the gap between the nation's ideals and Black workers' lives.

Parks was born in Fort Scott, Kansas, the youngest of 15 children. After his mother died in 1928, he moved as a teenager to St. Paul, Minnesota, to live with an older sister. He was soon forced out and became homeless. He attended Mechanic Arts High School and then enrolled at Central High School in 1929, but left a few months later as the Great Depression began. In the following years he worked many jobs, and in 1935 he became a porter and waiter on the Northern Pacific Railroad.

He bought a camera, taught himself photography, and began taking pictures in the Twin Cities, building a career as a fashion and portrait photographer. A Julius Rosenwald Fellowship brought him to Washington in 1942 to work with Roy Stryker at the Farm Security Administration, the federal agency that documented American life during the Depression. That is where he made American Gothic.

In 1948 he became the first African American staff photographer for Life magazine, where he worked until 1972. His photo essays covered fashion, poverty, and the civil rights movement. He was also a novelist, poet, and composer. He adapted his semi-autobiographical novel The Learning Tree into a 1969 film and composed its score, becoming the first African American to direct a major Hollywood movie. He went on to direct Shaft in 1971.
Parks died in 2006. His work is held by major institutions, including the Library of Congress and the National Gallery of Art.
keyFacts: 1912: Born November 30 in Fort Scott, Kansas.
1928: Moved to St. Paul; 1929: briefly attended Central High School.
1935: Began work as a railroad porter and waiter.
1942: Rosenwald Fellowship and Farm Security Administration work; made American Gothic, Washington, D.C.
1948–1972: Staff photographer at Life magazine, its first Black staff photographer.
1969: Directed The Learning Tree.
1971: Directed Shaft.
2006: Died.

people.name: Toni Stone
body: In 1953 the Indianapolis Clowns needed a new second baseman. The player who had held the position, Hank Aaron, had gone on to the major leagues with the Milwaukee Braves. The team signed Toni Stone, a woman from St. Paul. The Minnesota Historical Society calls her the first female professional baseball player in the Negro major leagues, and in an exhibition game she got a hit off the legendary pitcher Satchel Paige.

Some context helps here. Until 1947, Major League Baseball kept Black players out completely. In response, Black Americans built their own professional leagues, known as the Negro Leagues. These teams were important Black-owned businesses and a source of community pride. Many of baseball's greatest players played in them.

Stone was born Marcenia Lyle Stone in Bluefield, West Virginia. Her family moved to St. Paul when she was ten, and she grew up in the Rondo neighborhood. She played every sport she could, usually with boys. At sixteen, around 1937, she joined the Twin City Colored Giants, a barnstorming men's team.

She later moved to California and played briefly for the San Francisco Sea Lions and then, in 1949, for the New Orleans Creoles before signing with the Clowns. Before the 1954 season her contract went to the Kansas City Monarchs. She left after that season and moved to Oakland, where she worked as a nurse, and she kept coaching and playing semi-pro ball for years.

Her achievements were not widely recognized during her lifetime, but that has changed. St. Paul declared March 6, 1990, "Toni Stone Day," and later named a neighborhood ballpark Toni Stone Field. She was honored by the Baseball Hall of Fame in 1991 and inducted into the Women's Sports Hall of Fame in 1993. In 1997 St. Paul's History Theatre premiered a play about her life, Tomboy Stone. In 2021 she was inducted into the Minnesota Sports Hall of Fame.
keyFacts: 1921: Born July 17 as Marcenia Lyle Stone in Bluefield, West Virginia.
About 1931: Family moved to St. Paul.
About 1937: Joined the Twin City Colored Giants at age 16.
1949: Played for the New Orleans Creoles.
1953: Played second base for the Indianapolis Clowns, replacing Hank Aaron.
1954: Played for the Kansas City Monarchs, then retired from professional play.
1991: Honored by the Baseball Hall of Fame; 1993: Women's Sports Hall of Fame.
2021: Inducted into the Minnesota Sports Hall of Fame.
1996: Died.
people.connectToWork: When people built their own institution because a mainstream one shut them out, what does that tell you about the mainstream system you work in today?

people.name: Alan Page
body: On election night in November 1992, a former football star won a seat on the Minnesota Supreme Court. Alan Page became the first African American justice on the state's highest court. He was also one of the few justices in Minnesota history to first join the court by election rather than by appointment.

Many Minnesotans already knew Page from football. The Minnesota Vikings drafted him in the first round in 1967. As part of the team's famous "Purple People Eaters" defensive line, he became one of the best players in the game. In 1971 he became the first defensive player in NFL history to be named the league's Most Valuable Player. He was inducted into the Pro Football Hall of Fame in 1988.

While still playing, Page went to law school at the University of Minnesota. He practiced at the Minneapolis firm Lindquist and Vennum and then, from 1985, worked in the Minnesota Attorney General's Office before running for the Supreme Court. He served on the court from 1993 until he reached the mandatory retirement age in 2015.

Page has said that education changed his life, and he has worked to open that door for others. In 1988 he and his wife, Diane Sims Page, founded the Page Education Foundation, which gives grants to Minnesota students of color for college. By Carleton College's account, the foundation has supported more than 8,500 students. In return, each Page Scholar commits to volunteer and tutor children in kindergarten through 8th grade through a Service to Children Project.

In 2018 Page received the Presidential Medal of Freedom, the nation's highest civilian honor. In 2025 he expanded a foundation grant in honor of his former teammate Jim Marshall, so that recipients can use it for the full cost of attendance.
keyFacts: 1945: Born in Canton, Ohio.
1967: Drafted by the Minnesota Vikings.
1971: First defensive player named NFL Most Valuable Player.
1985: Joined the Minnesota Attorney General's Office.
1988: Co-founded the Page Education Foundation with Diane Sims Page; inducted into the Pro Football Hall of Fame.
1992: Elected as the first African American justice of the Minnesota Supreme Court; served 1993–2015.
2018: Received the Presidential Medal of Freedom.

people.name: Katherine Johnson
body: In February 1962, astronaut John Glenn was preparing to become the first American to orbit the Earth. NASA's new electronic computers had calculated his flight path, but Glenn wanted a person to check the numbers. He asked for Katherine Johnson. She checked the orbital equations by hand, and the flight went ahead.

Johnson was born in White Sulphur Springs, West Virginia, in 1918. She was gifted in math from a young age and was attending the high school on the campus of West Virginia State College, a historically Black college, by age 13. She graduated from the college with highest honors in 1937.

To understand her career, it helps to know about segregation at work. In 1953 Johnson joined the Langley laboratory of the agency that became NASA, in Hampton, Virginia. She worked as one of the "computers," women who did complex calculations by hand, in the all-Black West Area Computing section. Johnson's skill soon earned her a place working with the engineers on flight research.

She did the trajectory analysis for Alan Shepard's 1961 flight, the first American in space. After Glenn's orbit she helped calculate the trajectory for Apollo 11, the first mission to land people on the Moon. She also co-wrote research papers, which was rare for women at the agency at the time.

For many years, Johnson and her colleagues were not widely known. The 2016 book and film Hidden Figures changed that. In 2015 President Barack Obama awarded her the Presidential Medal of Freedom. NASA named its Katherine G. Johnson Computational Research Facility at Langley in her honor. She died in 2020 at the age of 101.
keyFacts: 1918: Born in White Sulphur Springs, West Virginia.
1937: Graduated from West Virginia State College.
1953: Began work at Langley, at the agency that later became NASA.
1961: Did trajectory analysis for Alan Shepard's Freedom 7 flight.
1962: Verified the orbital calculations for John Glenn's Friendship 7 flight.
2015: Received the Presidential Medal of Freedom.
2017: NASA's Katherine G. Johnson Computational Research Facility opened.
2020: Died at age 101.

people.name: Charles R. Drew
body: In 1940, as German bombs fell on Britain, New York hospitals set up a program called Blood for Britain to ship blood plasma overseas to treat the wounded. A young Black surgeon, Dr. Charles Drew, was its medical director and set the uniform procedures and standards it followed. By the time it ended in January 1941, the program had collected more than 14,000 donations. The methods Drew developed for safely collecting and storing plasma became a model for blood banking.

Drew was born in Washington, D.C., in 1904. He was a gifted athlete in school and at Amherst College. He went on to study medicine at McGill University in Canada. Later, at Columbia University, he researched how to store blood, and in 1940 he became the first African American to earn a doctorate in medical science from Columbia.

In 1941 Drew became assistant director of a pilot national blood banking program sponsored by the American Red Cross, where he introduced mobile donation stations later called bloodmobiles. The armed forces at first required the Red Cross to refuse blood from Black donors and later accepted it only if it was kept separate from white donors' blood. There was no scientific basis for this, and Drew criticized the policy publicly. He returned to Howard University, a historically Black university.

In October 1941, Drew became chair of Howard's Department of Surgery and chief of surgery at Freedmen's Hospital. Many consider his greatest legacy the generation of Black surgeons he trained there at a time when most medical schools and hospitals excluded them.

On April 1, 1950, while driving with three colleagues to the annual free clinic at John A. Andrew Hospital in Tuskegee, Alabama, Drew died from injuries suffered in a car accident near Burlington, North Carolina. He was 45. Schools, hospitals, and a medical university bear his name.
keyFacts: 1904: Born June 3 in Washington, D.C.
1933: Graduated from McGill University's medical school.
1940: Medical director of the Blood for Britain plasma program (ended January 1941).
1940: Earned a doctorate in medical science from Columbia University, the first African American to do so.
1941: Assistant director of the Red Cross pilot national blood bank program; spoke out against the segregation of blood.
October 1941: Chair of surgery at Howard University and chief of surgery at Freedmen's Hospital.
1950: Died after a car accident in North Carolina.

people.name: Madam C. J. Walker
body: In the early 1900s, women across the country began opening their doors to saleswomen trained in the "Walker System" of hair care. These agents, nearly all Black women, sold products and taught techniques door to door. For many, it was the first chance to earn a good living outside of domestic or farm work. The woman behind the system was Madam C. J. Walker.

She was born Sarah Breedlove on December 23, 1867, in Delta, Louisiana. Her parents had been enslaved on a Madison Parish plantation, and she was the first member of her family born into freedom. Orphaned before age seven, she married young, was widowed, and moved to St. Louis, where she worked as a laundress and cook.

Like many women of the time, she suffered from scalp problems and hair loss. In 1904 she began using and selling the hair products of businesswoman Annie Turnbo Malone, then developed her own. In 1905 she moved to Denver, married Charles Joseph Walker, took the name Madam C. J. Walker, and launched her own business.

Her business grew quickly. She trained agents and taught her methods. In 1910 she moved her operations to Indianapolis and built a factory for her Walker Manufacturing Company. She organized her agents and encouraged them to be active in their communities. In August 1917 she held her agents' first national convention, at Union Baptist Church in Philadelphia, with more than 200 women attending; delegates telegrammed President Wilson to protest the East St. Louis riots.

Walker became one of the wealthiest Black women of her time, with a fortune that topped $1 million, and she may have been the first American woman to become a millionaire through her own work. She gave to the NAACP, the YWCA, schools, and orphanages, paid tuition for Black students at Tuskegee Institute, and supported the anti-lynching movement. She died in 1919 at her estate, Villa Lewaro, in Irvington, New York.
keyFacts: 1867: Born Sarah Breedlove in Delta, Louisiana, to formerly enslaved parents.
1889: Moved to St. Louis.
1905: Moved to Denver and launched her own hair care business.
1910: Moved the company to Indianapolis and built a factory.
Trained many Black women as sales agents.
1917: First national convention of her agents, Philadelphia.
Funded the NAACP's anti-lynching work, the YWCA, and Black schools.
1919: Died May 25 at Villa Lewaro in Irvington, New York.

people.name: August Wilson
body: In 1982 a small Black theater company working out of a community center in St. Paul staged a new play called Black Bart and the Sacred Hills. The company was Penumbra Theatre, and the playwright was August Wilson. It was the first of his plays Penumbra produced, and the start of a relationship between a Minnesota stage and one of the most important American writers of the twentieth century.

Wilson was born on April 27, 1945, in Pittsburgh, and grew up in the Hill District of Pittsburgh, a historic Black neighborhood. He was largely self-taught, spending long hours at Pittsburgh's Carnegie Library, and began writing seriously at about age 20. He moved to St. Paul in the late 1970s. In St. Paul he took a job at the Science Museum of Minnesota, where he wrote children's plays based on Native American stories.

Penumbra was a natural home. It had been born inside a settlement house in St. Paul's Rondo neighborhood, and its founding principles came from the Black Arts Movement, which promoted art by Black artists, for Black audiences, about Black life. Wilson's plays did exactly that. While living in St. Paul during the 1980s he wrote several of his groundbreaking works.

Those plays became part of what is often called his Pittsburgh Cycle: ten plays, one for each decade of the twentieth century, tracing Black American life through ordinary people such as garbage collectors, musicians, cab drivers and boarding-house residents. Two of them won the Pulitzer Prize for Drama: Fences in 1987 and The Piano Lesson in 1990.

Wilson also spoke up for the theaters that nurtured him. In a 1996 speech he said, "Black theater in America is alive, it is vibrant, it is vital…it just isn't funded." Penumbra kept producing his work after he left Minnesota, including The Piano Lesson (1993), Seven Guitars, Two Trains Running (2003), Ma Rainey's Black Bottom (2014) and Jitney (2017).
Wilson died on October 2, 2005, in Seattle, at age 60. His cycle is now regularly performed across the country, and his St. Paul years are a reminder that Minnesota helped shape the American stage.
keyFacts: 1945: Born April 27 in Pittsburgh; grew up in Pittsburgh's Hill District.
Late 1970s: Moved to St. Paul.
1982: Penumbra staged Black Bart and the Sacred Hills, its first Wilson play.
1980s: Wrote several major plays while living in St. Paul.
1987: Pulitzer Prize for Drama for Fences.
1990: Pulitzer Prize for Drama for The Piano Lesson.
2005: Died October 2 in Seattle, age 60.

people.name: Ralph Bunche
body: In September 1948 the United Nations' mediator in Palestine was assassinated. His American deputy, Ralph Bunche, stepped in. After months of negotiation, he secured armistice agreements between Israel and the Arab states in 1949. The next year Bunche received the Nobel Peace Prize, the first African American to win it.

Bunche was born on August 7, 1904, in Detroit. After his parents died he was raised by his maternal grandmother in Los Angeles. He graduated first in his class from UCLA in 1927 with a degree in international relations, then went to Harvard, earning a master's degree in 1928 and a Ph.D. in government and international relations in 1934. Howard University describes him as the first African American to earn a doctorate in political science.

In the 1920s and 1930s, most American universities did not hire Black scholars. Historically Black colleges and universities, such as Howard, were where Black intellectuals taught, researched and trained the next generation. From 1928 to 1941 Bunche taught at Howard and built its political science department.

During World War II he moved into government work, and he helped create the UN itself. In 1945 he advised the U.S. delegation at the San Francisco Conference that drafted the UN Charter. In 1947 he became director of the UN Secretariat's Trusteeship Department, which oversaw territories moving toward self-government, at a time when many African and Asian peoples were seeking independence from colonial rule.

Bunche spent the rest of his career at the UN, working on crises in the Middle East, Africa and elsewhere. He also stayed connected to the civil rights movement at home, marching with Rev. Martin Luther King Jr. in Selma and Montgomery, Alabama.
He died on December 9, 1971, in New York, and is buried in Woodlawn Cemetery in the Bronx.
keyFacts: 1904: Born August 7 in Detroit, Michigan.
1927: Graduated first in his class from UCLA.
1934: Earned a Harvard Ph.D. in government and international relations.
1928–1941: Taught at Howard University and founded its political science department.
1945: Advised the U.S. delegation at the UN's San Francisco Conference.
1949: Secured armistice agreements as acting UN mediator.

people.name: Marian Anderson
body: On Easter Sunday, April 9, 1939, contralto Marian Anderson stood on the steps of the Lincoln Memorial in Washington, D.C., and sang to a crowd of more than 75,000 people. Howard University had asked to host her at Constitution Hall, owned by the Daughters of the American Revolution (DAR), and the request was refused because she was Black. First Lady Eleanor Roosevelt resigned from the DAR in protest. The outdoor concert became one of the defining moments of the early civil rights era.

Anderson was born on February 27, 1897, in Philadelphia, the granddaughter of enslaved Americans. Her musical life began in the Black church: at age 6 she started singing in the Union Baptist Church choir.

She built her career step by step. In 1917 she performed in Mendelssohn's Elijah at Jordan Hall in Boston, with the tenor Roland Hayes as a mentor. In 1919 she took an opera course at the Chicago Conservatory of Music and won the first award of the National Association of Negro Musicians. In 1927 she traveled to London to study, and in 1933 she began a European tour with concerts in Denmark, Norway, Sweden and Finland. She found wide acclaim in Europe before American venues fully opened to her.

After the 1939 concert, barriers continued to fall. On January 7, 1955, she became the first African American to perform on the main stage of the Metropolitan Opera in New York, singing the role of Ulrica in Verdi's Un Ballo in Maschera. In 1963 she received the Presidential Medal of Freedom, presented by President Lyndon B. Johnson after President Kennedy's assassination.
Anderson died on April 8, 1993, one day before the anniversary of her Lincoln Memorial concert. Her calm dignity on those steps remains a powerful image of protest through art.
keyFacts: 1897: Born February 27 in Philadelphia.
1903: Began singing in the Union Baptist Church choir.
1933: Began a European concert tour.
1939: Sang at the Lincoln Memorial on April 9 to more than 75,000 people after the DAR refused her Constitution Hall.
1955: First African American to perform on the Metropolitan Opera's main stage.
1963: Presidential Medal of Freedom.
1993: Died April 8.

people.name: Benjamin O. Davis Jr.
body: For four years at the U.S. Military Academy at West Point, from 1932 to 1936, almost no other cadet would speak to Benjamin O. Davis Jr. except on official business. This "silent treatment" was meant to drive the academy's only Black cadet out. Instead he graduated in June 1936, 35th in a class of 276, and went on to command the Tuskegee Airmen.

Davis was born in Washington, D.C., on December 18, 1912. His father, Benjamin O. Davis Sr., was a career Army officer who became the Army's first African American general. The son failed the West Point entrance exam in 1931 but passed easily the next year.

Davis’s career developed within U.S. armed forces that remained segregated until after World War II. Black soldiers were usually kept in separate units, and most were assigned to labor and support roles. The Army Air Corps at first did not train Black pilots at all. Under pressure, the military created a separate flight program at Tuskegee, Alabama.

In 1941 Davis was ordered to command the 99th Pursuit Squadron at Tuskegee Army Air Field. Its first pilots earned their wings on March 7, 1942, and the squadron flew its first combat mission on June 2, 1943, over Pantelleria in the Mediterranean. Davis was then recalled to command the larger 332nd Fighter Group, which moved to Italy in early 1944. He was promoted to colonel on May 29, 1944. The Tuskegee Airmen's record helped make the case for ending segregation in the military.

Davis became the first African American officer in the Air Force to reach the rank of general, and was promoted to lieutenant general in 1965. He retired in 1970 as a lieutenant general. On December 9, 1998, he was advanced to four-star general.
He died on July 4, 2002, at Walter Reed in Washington, D.C. The Tuskegee Airmen are now celebrated nationally, and Davis's leadership is central to their story.
keyFacts: 1912: Born December 18 in Washington, D.C.
1936: Graduated from West Point, 35th of 276, after four years of the silent treatment.
1941: Took command of the 99th Pursuit Squadron at Tuskegee.
1943: The 99th flew its first combat mission (June 2); Davis took command of the 332nd Fighter Group.
First African American Air Force officer to reach the rank of general.
1965: Promoted to lieutenant general.
1970: Retired as a lieutenant general.
1998: Advanced to four-star general on December 9.
2002: Died July 4 in Washington, D.C.

people.name: Mae Jemison
body: On September 12, 1992, the Space Shuttle Endeavour lifted off on mission STS-47. Aboard as a mission specialist was Dr. Mae Jemison, a physician and engineer. When the shuttle reached orbit, she became the first African American woman in space.

Jemison was born on October 17, 1956, in Decatur, Alabama. When she was about three and a half, her family moved to Chicago as part of the Great Migration, the movement of millions of Black Southerners to Northern and Western cities in search of opportunity and safety from Jim Crow. She started ballet at 8 and kept a lifelong love of dance alongside science.

She graduated from Chicago's Morgan Park High School at 16, in 1973. At Stanford University she earned a B.S. in chemical engineering in 1977 and, in NASA's words, fulfilled the requirements for a B.A. in African and Afro-American Studies. She went on to earn her medical degree from Cornell Medical School in 1981, spending one summer working in Kenya with the African Medical Education and Research Foundation.

In 1983 she joined the Peace Corps as a medical officer, and at 26 she became the Area Peace Corps Medical Officer for Sierra Leone and Liberia. She applied to NASA's astronaut program in 1985; the program paused after the Challenger explosion in 1986. In 1987 she was one of 15 people chosen for Astronaut Group 12 from more than 2,000 applicants. Her flight on STS-47 lasted from September 12 to 20, 1992.

Jemison left NASA in 1993. She then founded an international science camp, The Earth We Share, and a consulting firm, the Jemison Group, and became a professor at Dartmouth College. In 2012 she created the 100 Year Starship initiative, which aims to make human travel to other stars possible within a century.
Her career links science, medicine, the arts and service to communities in Africa and the United States.
keyFacts: 1956: Born October 17 in Decatur, Alabama; raised in Chicago.
1977: Stanford B.S. in chemical engineering; also fulfilled the requirements for a B.A. in African and Afro-American Studies.
1981: M.D. from Cornell Medical School.
1983: Joined the Peace Corps as a medical officer (Sierra Leone and Liberia).
1987: Selected for NASA Astronaut Group 12.
1992: Flew on STS-47 (September 12–20), the first African American woman in space.
1993: Left NASA.
2012: Created the 100 Year Starship initiative.

people.name: Brad Lomax
body: In April 1977, disabled activists took over the federal building in San Francisco. They were demanding that the government finally enforce Section 504 of the Rehabilitation Act, which bans disability discrimination by programs that receive federal money. Among them was Brad Lomax, a young Black man who used a wheelchair because of multiple sclerosis. Lomax persuaded the Black Panther Party to back the protest, and the Panthers brought hot meals every day. PBS puts the sit-in at 26 days.

Lomax was born in North Philadelphia in 1950 and enrolled at Howard University after finishing high school in 1967. At Howard he joined the Black Panthers, and he helped found the party's Washington, D.C., chapter, where he worked to build a free health clinic. He moved to Oakland in 1973. There he saw that the Berkeley Center for Independent Living was not reaching the largely Black neighborhoods of East Oakland. With Panther support, he ran the East Oakland Center for Independent Living from 1975 to 1977. He died on August 28, 1984, of complications of MS. PBS describes him as devoted to the work rather than the limelight.

Enrolled at Howard University after graduating from high school in 1967.
Helped found the D.C. chapter of the Black Panther Party.
1975–1977: East Oakland Center for Independent Living.

people.name: Johnnie Lacy
body: Johnnie Lacy was born in 1937 and spent her childhood in Arkansas and Louisiana during segregation. In 1947, when she was 10, her family moved to California, where she lived in McCloud. She attended Chico State from 1954 to 1956 and was studying toward nursing when she contracted polio in 1956, at 19. From 1958 to 1960 she majored in speech therapy at San Francisco State, a campus that was not accessible. The department head tried to block her enrollment, and she was not allowed to take part in graduation. She worked in anti-poverty programs for the Oakland Economic Development Council from 1965 to 1968. As a Black woman who used a wheelchair, Lacy faced both racial and disability discrimination in higher education and in employment.

She went on to help found the Center for Independent Living in Berkeley. In 1981 she became executive director of Community Resources for Independent Living (CRIL) in Hayward. She led it until 1994, raising $350,000 and securing city funding for a center built in 1984. The California State Senate named her Woman of the Year in 1988. She later served on Hayward commissions and on San Francisco's Mayor's Disability Council. She died in 2010 at age 73.

Lacy spoke about being excluded from Black spaces because of her disability and from disability spaces because of her race. She pushed the independent living movement to face racism within its own ranks.

Contracted polio in 1956, at 19, while studying toward nursing.

Died 2010, age 73.

1988: California State Senate Woman of the Year.

institutions.name: Penumbra Theatre
body: In 1976 the Hallie Q. Brown Community Center, a St. Paul settlement house serving the Black community, hired a young graduate student named Lou Bellamy to run a cultural arts program. Bellamy named the project Penumbra. In 1977 the company staged its first productions, Eden by Steve Carter and The Taking of Miss Janie by Ed Bullins, at the center, with Bellamy in the lead role.

Penumbra grew out of the Black Arts Movement, which called for professional theater that explored the African American experience on its own terms. It became the artistic home of August Wilson, staging his Black Bart and the Sacred Hills in 1982 and producing many of his plays in later decades.

In 1990 Penumbra separated from Hallie Q. Brown and became its own nonprofit. It has had hard times, including layoffs and a canceled season reported in 2012. In 2012 the board chose Bellamy's daughter, Sarah Bellamy, to succeed him; she became president and artistic director in January 2017.

In 2020, after the murder of George Floyd, the company announced its transition to the Penumbra Center for Racial Healing, extending its work from the stage into community programs. Penumbra remains in its original St. Paul home and is marking its 50th season.

1982: First August Wilson play.

institutions.name: Minnesota Spokesman-Recorder
body: In the summer of 1934, Cecil Newman published the first edition of the Minneapolis Spokesman, soon followed by the St. Paul Recorder. Newman, who had come to Minneapolis from Kansas City in 1922 and worked as a railroad porter, pledged that his papers would speak out against injustice.

He meant it. In spring 1935 the Spokesman reported that local breweries, including Hamm's and Gluek's, were hiring new workers after Prohibition but hiring no African Americans. Newman called for a boycott. In 1943 his lobbying led to a large increase in Black employment at the Twin Cities Army Ammunition Plant in New Brighton. In 1948 he became president of the Minneapolis Urban League. The paper also gave the young photographer Gordon Parks his start.

In 1958 Newman and builder Wayne Glanton built a new home for both papers in South Minneapolis. After Newman's death in 1976, his widow, Launa Q. Newman, carried on the work. The paper itself dates the merger of the two papers into the Minnesota Spokesman-Recorder to 2000; WCCO says the merger came under Newman's widow, and the City of Minneapolis says Newman merged them. His granddaughter, Tracey Williams-Dillard, is CEO and publisher. In 2015 the Minneapolis City Council designated the building a historic landmark. The city calls it the longest-running African American newspaper in the state.
keyFacts: 1934: Minneapolis Spokesman and St. Paul Recorder founded by Cecil Newman.
1935: Called for a brewery hiring boycott.
1958: Moved into its building at 3744 Fourth Avenue South.

institutions.name: Rondo neighborhood and Rondo Days
body: In the 1930s, half of St. Paul's Black residents lived in Rondo, a neighborhood named for Joseph Rondeau, who bought land there in 1872. It was a full community, with businesses and social clubs such as the Credjafawn Social Club, which opened in 1928 and later ran a cooperative grocery store, and the Booker T. Café and Tavern, opened in 1949. Toni Stone, profiled on this page, grew up there.

In 1956 the city planning board chose a route for Interstate 94 straight through Rondo. Residents formed the Rondo–St. Anthony Improvement Association that January to defend their homes and businesses, but construction began that September. When Rev. George Davis refused to leave his home, police removed him. The freeway, built from 1956 to 1968, cut the neighborhood in half. Sources differ on how many it displaced: MNopedia's overview says more than 600 residents, AARP says more than 1,000 families and more than 100 Black-owned businesses, and the Spokesman-Recorder and MPR News say thousands of residents.

The community kept its memory alive. In July 1983 the first Rondo Days Festival was held, according to MNopedia and organizer Gayle Smaller (AARP gives both 1982 and 1983); MNopedia describes it as the largest African American festival in the state. The organization Rondo Avenue Inc. worked to commemorate and revive the neighborhood's history, and in 2006 the Rondo Community Outreach Library opened.
keyFacts: 1930s: Half of St. Paul's Black population lived in Rondo.
1956: I-94 route adopted; construction began in September.
1968: I-94 corridor opened on December 9.
1983: First Rondo Days Festival in July.
2006: Rondo Community Outreach Library opened.

disability.intro: This is background for preparing questions. It does not describe any person or family. Here, African American means Black Americans descended from people enslaved in the U.S., who differ widely in faith, generation, income, region of origin and experience with public systems. We did not find a Minnesota-based study of how African American Minnesotans understand disability. The research below is national, mostly from the South or East Coast, and often about one condition.
questions: How do you and your family understand what's going on? What words do you use for it?
Has anyone given you a diagnosis or a label? Do you agree with it, and has it helped or got in the way?
What would you want a disability label or assessment to open up for you? Is there anything you worry it might close off?
Who do you usually turn to for help: family, friends, church, others? Would you like any of them involved?
Have past experiences with doctors, schools, police or county services affected how you feel about getting services? What would make this feel safer?
What times, places and ways of meeting work for you, including work hours, transportation, and phone or in person?
Is faith or a congregation important to you, and would it help to connect services with it?
Do you prefer "disabled person", "person with a disability", or other words?

context.heading: What studies have asked about explanations and first steps
body: A 2008 conference survey of 80 parents of children with autism, aged 5 to 14 (40 African American, 40 white), reported that a significant number of parents across the sample held supernatural beliefs about cause. In both groups, beliefs about cause predicted the kind of help parents said they would seek. It is a small sample and a conference abstract, and it says nothing about any one family.

A 2022 Kennedy Krieger Institute article reports that Black parents may first take a concern about a child's development or behavior to a trusted community member, often a faith leader. This does not mean a family rejects medical care. Ask how the person understands the condition. Explanations vary with generation, denomination, education and past experience with health systems.

sources.label: Maina, Weru and Brown, International Meeting for Autism Research (2008), abstract
Kennedy Krieger Institute, Building Connections in Black Communities (2022)

context.heading: Family, church and formal services
body: In a mixed-methods study in rural Georgia, 163 African American mothers took a survey and 21 were interviewed about help for adolescents with mental health needs. Mothers most often named family, church and schools as supports, and most said they had confidence that mental health providers could help (Murry and colleagues, 2011).

A survey of 269 Southern churches, published in 2002, found that Black churches offered significantly more mental health and social programs than white churches, and that few churches had formal links with health or mental health providers (Blank and colleagues). Neither study identifies who helps any particular person. Ask each person who helps them and who they want involved in decisions; include a pastor or congregation only with the person's consent.

sources.label: Murry, Heflinger, Suiter and Brody, Journal of Youth and Adolescence (2011), abstract
Blank, Mahmood, Fox and Guterbock, American Journal of Public Health (2002)

context.heading: Stigma, mistrust and system barriers
body: In the same Georgia study, community stigma toward children with mental health problems and their families was often named as a barrier. Cultural mistrust was one of the two most often named barriers in the survey, but it was not universal in that sample. Mistrust has roots in documented abuses, such as the Tuskegee Study (1932 to 1972), and in current experiences of bias. Treat it as a reasonable response to history, not a deficit.

The Kennedy Krieger article cites research that Black children with autism are diagnosed later than white peers. It names practical barriers: insurance, transportation, bias, misunderstandings, and clinic hours that conflict with work. Check these system explanations before reading a missed appointment as cultural.

sources.label: Murry, Heflinger, Suiter and Brody, Journal of Youth and Adolescence (2011), abstract
Kennedy Krieger Institute, Building Connections in Black Communities (2022)

context.heading: Words, format and how to work
body: We found no research on terms for disability specific to this community, so none are offered here. Follow each person's own preference. Avoid outdated clinical terms that still appear in older studies.

Explain clearly what information is shared, with whom, and why. Use plain language, confirm understanding without talking down, and offer written follow-up. Do not assume an interpreter is or is not needed. Offer ASL interpreters to Black Deaf people, and ask whether they prefer an interpreter familiar with Black ASL.

sources.label: Kennedy Krieger Institute, Building Connections in Black Communities (2022)

context.heading: Black disabled leadership and who is missing
body: Johnnie Lacy, profiled on this page, spoke about exclusion from Black spaces because of disability and from disability spaces because of race. Brad Lomax brought Black Panther Party support to the 504 sit-in and ran a center in East Oakland because the Berkeley center was not reaching those neighborhoods.

We did not find a Minnesota organization led by Black disabled people that serves African American families, though the search was limited. The National Black Disability Coalition is the main national route, and the St. Paul/Minneapolis Black Deaf Advocates is a local one. Do not treat any one person or organization as speaking for everyone.

organizations.intro: Since the early 1900s, African American Minnesotans have organized through churches such as Pilgrim Baptist, settlement houses and community centers, and civil rights and economic groups. In 2026 four Black-led nonprofits formed the Legacy Stabilization Collaborative to strengthen their infrastructure. The list below is not complete, and listing here says nothing about who a person trusts.

entries.purpose: Formally organized in 1866, with roots in 1863 in Robert Hickman's group of people who escaped slavery. The first African American Baptist church in Minnesota, with a long civic role in school integration, voting rights and Rondo advocacy.

entries.purpose: A medical, dental and mental health center and human-service agency. Runs the African-American Men Project for Hennepin County men 18 and older, with peer support and job-finding help.

entries.purpose: Founded in 1976. Culturally specific recovery services for African Americans, including a 90-day inpatient program, outpatient care, transitional housing, peer recovery, and walk-in assessments for opioid treatment.

entries.location: St. Paul, Amherst H. Wilder Foundation

By its own account it began in 2000 as a spin-off of the New Jersey Black Disability Coalition, after that group's 10 years of work. Its work includes Black Disability Studies, family mentoring, employment references, and education and referral.
